clue.text: Hit fly — messy!

blocks.note: to hit with an open hand
to fly is to rush or hurry off

explanation.surface: Someone swats a fly and leaves a smear on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit fly' reads as swatting an insect, but both words are verbs: strike, then hurry away.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash work is careless and hurried, so the adjective is a close synonym for untidy or sloppy.

clue.text: Join some unit in Kenya on the climb

indicators.note: taking only some of a run of letters means the result sits inside the words
in a down clue, climbing means reading from the bottom upward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the three words

explanation.surface: Signing up with a military unit stationed in Kenya, maybe a mountain unit.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'unit in Kenya' and read upward in this down entry; 'Join' is a verb, as in knitting bones together.
explanation.definitionFit: Broken bones knit as they heal, and to knit things is to unite or bind them closely together.

clue.text: Capital where fighting witnessed

explanation.surface: A capital city where battles were seen, apt for a city wrecked in the Second World War.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is historically apt: the city was largely destroyed in 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: Warsaw is the capital city of Poland, so it is an example of a national capital.

clue.text: Very old goat seen on the rocks

indicators.note: something on the rocks is wrecked or in ruins, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: An ancient mountain goat spotted clambering among the crags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rocks' is literally where a goat lives, which hides its job as the signal; 'seen' is both link and fodder here, giving the second half of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stone-age is used informally for anything hopelessly old-fashioned or primitive, from the prehistoric period of stone tools.

clue.text: Where television aerial may be free

blocks.note: literally: fixed up on the roof of a building
idiom for something given at the expense of the establishment

explanation.surface: Someone is told their TV aerial might come at no cost.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is taken literally, the second is the pub or restaurant idiom for no charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinks served on the house are paid for by the bar, so the phrase means without charge to the customer.

clue.text: Marker certainly not for the French flag

blocks.note: a pen is something that marks paper

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to use a French flag as a marker post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the French' asks for the French translation of the emphatic refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long narrow triangular banner, traditionally carried on a knight's lance, so it is a type of pennant.

clue.text: Insect burrowing into unremarkable fruit

indicators.note: a creature that burrows into something ends up enclosed within it

explanation.surface: A bug tunnels into a dull-looking piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a literal grub in the fruit; the insect is a tiny crossword favourite placed inside a word for ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: The plantain is a starchy relative of the banana, usually cooked, so it is a tropical fruit.

clue.text: Home in which I chill, initially, most gorgeous

indicators.note: at the start, so only the opening letter of that word is used
a place in which things sit holds them inside it

explanation.surface: Someone relaxing at their lovely home, which they call the most gorgeous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chill' looks like relaxing, but only its first letter joins the I inside a bird's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicest is the superlative of nice, so it means most pleasant or attractive, matching the superlative in the clue.

clue.text: Finally kaput, mend a broken bike

indicators.note: at the end, so only the last letter of the word is kept
something broken has its parts out of place, so the letters must be put back in new order

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bicycle has finally given up and someone is told to repair it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mend' and 'broken' fit the repair story, yet one supplies letters and the other signals rearranging them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandem is a bicycle built for two riders sitting one behind the other, so it is a kind of bike.

clue.text: See caps reversed

indicators.note: turned to face the other way, so the letters are read back to front

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at baseball caps worn backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a verb here, as in catching sight of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to notice or catch sight of it, a common synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Part of timer used

blocks.note: the pointer on a clock face that counts the seconds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Used' looks like a verb about the timer but is an adjective for pre-owned goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods bought from a previous owner are described as pre-owned or not new; a clock face also carries this pointer.

clue.text: Grave punch-up in tavern?

explanation.surface: A serious brawl breaks out in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A fight in a tavern is read as a 'bar row', so the place comes first; 'Grave' looks like an adjective for serious but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow is an ancient burial mound of earth or stones, so it is a kind of tomb.

clue.text: Great African swimmer performing heroics on crossing river

indicators.note: something performing puts on an act, so the letters are made to take a new form

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A big African animal swims heroically across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the first two words plus the river letter is rearranged; the hippo is the obvious river swimmer, but the letters spell its horned neighbour, which also swims well.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros is a huge horned herbivore of the African savanna that can wade and swim across rivers.

clue.text: Super activity on court?

blocks.note: second meaning: hitting hard overhead shots in tennis

explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court; the question mark flags the playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the word for terrific or marvellous, and in tennis a smash is a powerful overhead shot.

clue.text: Peak reached by rowing crew after end of stretch

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: a racing boat with eight oarsmen, and its crew

explanation.surface: A boat crew reaches its peak form after the final stretch of the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' is the closing part of a race in the surface; in rowing an eight is both the boat and the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: The height of something is its peak or highest point, as in the height of fame or success.

clue.text: Pain in the neck — or just above it?

definitions.text: Pain in the neck — or just above it?

blocks.note: surface reading: a nuisance or irritating problem
setter's reading: a literal pain located in the skull, sitting just above the neck

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for a nuisance is taken literally and then moved up an inch to the skull, which gives a second word for both a nuisance and a pain there.
explanation.definitionFit: A troublesome problem is called a headache, and it is also literally an ache in the cranium above the neck.

clue.text: Navy led by true revolutionary in retreat

indicators.note: revolution turns things over, so these letters are overturned into a new order

explanation.surface: A fleet commanded by a genuine rebel is falling back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Led by' puts the shuffled word in front of the navy. RN is the usual abbreviation for Britain's Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words can mean going back, as a withdrawal or a trip back home; return is used as a verb or noun for going back.

clue.text: Toxic substance with carbon monoxide in it, figure will claim

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it
to claim something is to take hold of it, so the outer piece grips the inner

blocks.note: the chemical formula for carbon monoxide

explanation.surface: A poisonous gas mixture that, statistics will claim, kills people, like cigarette smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: The gas formula goes inside 'it', then that combined chunk goes inside a number.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicotine is the poisonous alkaloid found in tobacco, used historically as an insecticide, so it is a toxin.

clue.text: Gift set newly secured by tied ribbon?

indicators.note: made new again, so the letters are reformed in a fresh order
something secured by a tie is held fast inside it

explanation.surface: A present set wrapped and fastened with a ribbon bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gift' reads as a noun for the present, but it is the verb, to give.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestow is to confer or present something as an honour, so it works as the verb to give.

clue.text: Meeting outside of college, set off

indicators.note: lying outside something means wrapping around it

blocks.note: an appointment, especially a romantic one
ETON is a famous English private school, Eton College

explanation.surface: People meet outside a college and then head off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' looks like leaving on a journey, but it means triggering an explosion. Eton College is an English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb or charge is to make it explode, which is exactly to detonate it.

clue.text: Scratching head, imagine cryptic puzzle

indicators.note: scratching out the head removes the first letter
something cryptic is obscured, so the letters are disguised in a new order

blocks.note: the word without its opening letter

explanation.surface: A solver scratches their head over a cryptic crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: The head-scratching solver picture hides an instruction to drop a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or riddle that is hard to understand, so it is a synonym for a puzzle.

clue.text: Rip off wool

blocks.note: first meaning: to swindle or overcharge
second meaning: a sheep's woolly coat

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests tearing wool off a sheep; the two senses are cheating someone and a sheep's coat.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to cheat them of money, and a fleece is the coat shorn from a sheep.

clue.text: Left hoof around right, stumbling finally

indicators.note: at the end, so the last letter of the word is kept
going around something means enclosing it

blocks.note: to hoof it is to go on foot
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An animal stumbles on its left hoof as it goes round to the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' sits beside 'right' as a direction, but it is the past tense meaning failed to bring something.
explanation.definitionFit: If you left your keys at home you forgot them, so the past tenses share the sense of failing to take along.

clue.text: In prodding damp flower, one enjoying bouquet?

indicators.note: a prod pokes into something, so one piece is pushed inside another

explanation.surface: Someone pokes at a wet bloom while sniffing a bouquet of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' here is a real bloom, not a river; 'bouquet' is the scent of a wine, not a bunch of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine's aroma is called its bouquet, so a professional sampler of wines savours that scent as part of the job.

clue.text: Repeated cheers, and I’m off!

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks, as is cheers

explanation.surface: Someone says thanks twice on their way out of the door.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain both cheers and ta are casual ways of saying thank you; doubling the short word gives a cheerful farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is a casual British goodbye, said by someone leaving, so it stands in for the exclamation of departure.

clue.text: Input category

blocks.note: first meaning: to key text into a computer
second meaning: a kind or sort

explanation.walkthrough: 'Input' reads as a noun beside 'category', but it is the verb for keying in text.
explanation.definitionFit: One enters text at a keyboard by typing it, and a sort or class of things is also called a type.

clue.text: Flat male accommodated in very hot, unfortunately

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome has gone wrong, so the letters go awry into a new order
to be accommodated in a place is to be housed inside it

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A man housed in a sweltering flat, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment, matching 'accommodated', but it is the adjective for level and even.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth surface has no bumps or ridges, so it is level and even like a flat one.

clue.text: Massive weight originally on one foot

indicators.note: at its origin, meaning the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: moving by jumping on a single leg

explanation.surface: A huge weight balanced on a single foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On one foot' is not a position for the weight but a way of moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Whopping is an informal intensifier for something huge or enormous, so it matches the adjective for great size.
